name: Sapporo & Otaru
tagline: A northern city of great food, night views and canals, and two nights is plenty
intro: Soup curry, Genghis Khan lamb, miso ramen and seafood rice bowls are all within walking distance of each other, and the evening ends with the Mt. Moiwa night view and a late-night 'shime parfait.' Otaru, with its canal and glass crafts, is a 40-minute train ride away for an easy day trip, and Jozankei Onsen is an hour by bus for autumn leaves and open-air baths. It suits first-time visitors to Hokkaido, two women traveling together, and families with kids.
season_notes: Spring (Apr-May): cherry blossoms come in early May, right after the snow melts, so the streets can feel a bit bare. Summer (Jun-Aug): no rainy season and pleasantly cool, ideal for strolling and the Odori beer garden (Jul-Aug). Autumn (Sep-Oct): the Hokkaido University ginkgo trees and Jozankei foliage peak in mid to late October. Winter (Dec-Feb): the Snow Festival is in early February; the paths are slippery, so shoes with ice grips are a must.
airport_access/0/note: 6 trains an hour during the day (about every 10 to 12 minutes). Reserved-seat u-Seat costs extra. The special rapid is the fastest at 33 minutes
airport_access/1/note: Some trains run straight through Sapporo Station to Otaru. Fare to be confirmed
airport_access/2/note: Some routes stop right at your hotel, which is handy with heavy luggage. Can be delayed by road conditions. Fare to be confirmed
getting_around: The core of the city (Sapporo Station, Odori, Susukino and Tanukikoji) sits within 1.5 km north to south, so the single Namboku subway line plus walking is enough. In winter, the underground walkway (Chika-ho) lets you go indoors from Sapporo Station all the way to Susukino. Use JR for Otaru, a bus for Jozankei, and the streetcar plus a free shuttle for Mt. Moiwa.
transport_pass: A subway-only one-day ticket is ¥830, and the Donichika Kippu for weekends and holidays is ¥520 (2024 prices; 2026 fares to be confirmed). It only pays off if you ride three or more times a day, and simply tapping with Suica in your iPhone Wallet is often easier.
spots/0/desc: The gateway to Hokkaido. The 2nd and 3rd floors of the domestic terminal are packed with food and souvenir shops such as Royce' Chocolate World, Ramen Dojo and Kinotoya, so the airport alone can fill half a day.
spots/0/access: Take the JR Rapid Airport from JR New Chitose Airport Station on the B1 level
spots/0/hours: International departures lobby always open; shops are generally 8:00–20:00
spots/0/tip: Finish your souvenir shopping on the domestic terminal's 2nd floor, then take the connecting walkway to the international terminal. Aim to arrive 2 hours before departure.
spots/0/kid_tip: The Doraemon Waku Waku Sky Park and a Studio Ghibli shop on the domestic 3rd floor are big hits with kids.
spots/1/desc: The central hub where JR, the subway and buses meet. Stellar Place, Daimaru and Esta are attached to the station, so shopping and dining are all under one roof.
spots/1/access: End of the JR Rapid Airport line; Sapporo Station on the Namboku and Toho subway lines
spots/1/tip: Buy souvenirs in the Daimaru basement food hall, and clothes and sundries at Stellar Place. Coin lockers fill up early in the morning, so leaving your bags at your hotel is safer.
spots/1/kid_tip: Stellar Place has a restaurant floor on the 6th floor, and Daimaru has a nursing room.
spots/2/desc: A 1.5 km ribbon-shaped park running east to west through the city center. It is the main venue of the February Snow Festival, hosts the beer garden in July and August, and turns gold and red with ginkgo and maple leaves in October.
spots/2/access: Directly connected to Odori subway station
spots/2/tip: Walk west to the Sapporo Historical Museum, enjoying the fountains and the corn food carts (summer to autumn), and an hour passes quickly.
spots/2/kid_tip: There is a playground with slides at blocks 9 to 10 on the west side.
spots/3/desc: A 147 m tower at the east end of Odori Park. From the 90 m observation deck you look down on Sapporo's signature view, with the park stretching out in a straight line.
spots/3/access: 1-minute walk from Exit 27 of Odori subway station
spots/3/tip: Many people say the photo looking up at it from the park is prettier than the view from the deck, so if you are short on time, just snapping the exterior is enough. The elevator is suspended in strong wind.
spots/3/kid_tip: Elementary and junior high students ¥600; free for preschoolers.
spots/4/desc: Built in 1878, it is the oldest clock tower in Japan. It looks small among the surrounding office buildings, but inside you can see exhibits from the pioneer era and the clock's mechanism.
spots/4/access: 5-minute walk from Odori subway station, 10 minutes from Sapporo Station
spots/4/tip: The 2nd-floor terrace of the Sapporo MN Building across the street is the classic photo spot. It stays open until 20:00 on the first Monday of each month.
spots/4/kid_tip: Free for high school students and younger.
spots/5/desc: The red-brick former prefectural office built in 1888. After five years of restoration it reopened in July 2025, adding a Hokkaido history exhibit and a tour of the octagonal tower.
spots/5/access: 8-minute walk from the south exit of JR Sapporo Station, 7 minutes from Odori subway station
spots/5/tip: The front-garden pond and ginkgo trees are especially pretty in autumn, and the building is lit up at night. The octagonal tower tour requires a separate fee and a reservation.
spots/5/kid_tip: Free for junior high students and younger.
spots/6/desc: A covered arcade running about 900 m from 1-chome to 7-chome. With Don Quijote, drugstores and souvenir shops, you can shop even when it rains or snows.
spots/6/access: 3-minute walk from Susukino or Odori subway station; streetcar stop Tanukikoji
spots/6/hours: Shops generally 10:00–22:00; Don Quijote open 24 hours
spots/6/tip: Split your drugstore shopping into one trip at night and one on your last day to spread out the luggage. Bring your passport for tax-free purchases.
spots/6/kid_tip: It is an arcade, so it is easy to get around with a stroller.
spots/7/desc: The big neon intersection that symbolizes Hokkaido's largest entertainment district. Ramen Alley, Genghis Khan restaurants and seafood izakaya are all within a 5-minute walk.
spots/7/access: Directly connected to Susukino station on the Namboku subway line
spots/7/tip: The mall Kokono Susukino, which opened in 2023, is right at the intersection and makes a good rainy-day refuge.
spots/7/kid_tip: There are many touts after 10 p.m., so with kids, head back to your hotel early after dinner.
spots/8/desc: A market more than 100 years old in the middle of downtown. You can have a kaisendon topped with sea urchin, salmon roe and crab from early morning, and the dried fish and melon stalls are fun to browse too.
spots/8/access: 5-minute walk from Odori or Bus Center-mae subway station
spots/8/hours: About 7:00–18:00 (varies by shop; restaurants open around 7 a.m.)
spots/8/tip: If you arrive before 8 a.m., you can eat without a line. With crab, check the weight before haggling over the price.
spots/8/kid_tip: The fishy smell is strong, so take a short look around and then head to a restaurant.
spots/9/desc: A 531 m-high observatory counted among Japan's 'New Three Great Night Views.' You ride up by transferring between the ropeway and the mini cable car, and the key is to go up at dusk and watch the sunset turn into the night view.
spots/9/access: Get off the streetcar at Ropeway-iriguchi, then take the free shuttle bus for 5 minutes to the base station
spots/9/closed: Dec 31, Jan 1, and one maintenance closure a year (in 2026, Apr 1–23)
spots/9/tip: The summit is more than 5 degrees colder than downtown, so a scarf and gloves are a must. The ¥2,100 round trip is the combined ropeway and cable car fare. There is word that the base parking lot will charge a fee from September 2026, so rental car users should confirm (to be confirmed).
spots/9/kid_tip: Children's round trip is ¥1,050. The 'Bell of Happiness' photo spot at the summit is popular with kids.
spots/10/desc: A ginkgo tunnel about 380 m long inside the campus. It peaks in bright yellow in late October, and a loop that also takes in the poplar avenue and the bust of Dr. Clark makes a one-hour stroll.
spots/10/access: 5-minute walk from Kita-juni-jo station on the Namboku subway line, 10 minutes from the north exit of Sapporo Station
spots/10/hours: Always open (the campus is open to the public)
spots/10/tip: On peak ginkgo weekends, traffic is restricted and a light-up event is held. You can pick up snacks at the Seicomart on campus.
spots/10/kid_tip: The path is flat, so strollers are fine. The General Museum (free) has dinosaur fossils.
spots/11/desc: The largest shrine, dedicated to the guardian deities of Hokkaido's development. Surrounded by the Maruyama primeval forest, it is a beloved walking spot for cherry and plum blossoms in early May and autumn leaves in October.
spots/11/access: 15-minute walk from Maruyama-koen station on the Tozai subway line
spots/11/hours: Generally 6:00–17:00 (winter 7:00–16:00, varies by month, to be confirmed)
spots/11/tip: The 'Hanjitsu' rice cakes sold at the Rokkatei Shrine Tea Shop on the grounds are available only here. Pair it with Morihiko's main shop for a half-day course.
spots/11/kid_tip: Maruyama Zoo is a 10-minute walk away, so the two combine nicely.
spots/12/desc: A municipal zoo famous for its polar bears and elephants. Many exhibits are indoors, so you can enjoy it in winter and on rainy days too.
spots/12/access: 5 minutes by bus or a 15-minute walk from Maruyama-koen subway station
spots/12/hours: Mar–Oct 9:30–16:30, Nov–Feb 9:30–16:00 (last entry 30 minutes before closing)
spots/12/closed: 2nd and 4th Wednesday of each month (1st and 4th in August; next day if a holiday), Mon–Fri of the week of the 2nd Wednesday in April and November, Dec 29–31
spots/12/tip: E-tickets have been sold since March 2026. The polar bears are most active in the morning.
spots/12/kid_tip: Free for junior high students and younger. Stroller rental is available.
spots/13/desc: A theme park built around the factory of Shiroi Koibito, Hokkaido's signature sweet. With European-style gardens, roses and a cookie-making experience, it pleases both photo lovers and kids.
spots/13/access: 7-minute walk from Miyanosawa station on the Tozai subway line
spots/13/tip: The paid tour area reopens after a renovation on July 30, 2026. Prices and hours after the renovation are to be confirmed. The garden and shops are free, so shopping alone is worth the trip.
spots/13/kid_tip: ¥400 for ages 4 through junior high. Reserve the cookie-making experience in advance.
spots/14/desc: Japan's only beer museum, housed in a red-brick factory from 1890. A July 2026 renovation refreshed the exhibits and guided tours, and it leads right into Genghis Khan at the neighboring beer garden.
spots/14/access: 10-minute walk from Higashi-kuyakusho-mae station on the Toho subway line; or take the bus from Sapporo Station to 'Sapporo Biergarten'
spots/14/closed: Dec 31, temporary closures (some sources mention Monday closures, to be confirmed)
spots/14/tip: Based on the official announcement, after the July 2026 renovation admission is ¥1,000, and a premium tour with two tastings is ¥2,000 (reservation required). Tours are closed on Mondays.
spots/14/kid_tip: ¥500 for junior high students. A non-alcoholic drink or juice can be chosen instead of the tasting.
spots/15/desc: A gorge hot-spring town one hour by bus from downtown Sapporo. The leaves peak in mid-October, and you can enjoy foot baths and day-trip hot springs along the Futami Park suspension bridge and the kappa statues.
spots/15/access: About 75 minutes by Jotetsu Bus from Sapporo Station Bus Terminal (around ¥950), or about 60 minutes by the reservation-only direct Kappa Liner (fare to be confirmed)
spots/15/tip: The ¥1,000 is a rough day-bath price (estimate). Weekend buses in the foliage season fill up, so leave early in the morning. If you stay overnight, you can also enjoy a leisurely multi-course dinner.
spots/15/kid_tip: Free foot baths around town and hunting for kappa statues are a game kids love.
spots/16/desc: A huge art park designed by the sculptor Isamu Noguchi. A glass pyramid, an artificial mountain and fountains sit on wide lawns, making it great for photos.
spots/16/access: About 25 minutes by bus from Kanjo-dori-higashi station on the Toho subway line
spots/16/closed: Glass Pyramid closed Mondays (next day if a holiday); the park has no regular closing day (to be confirmed)
spots/16/tip: The park is large, so rental bikes (paid) are efficient. It is windy, so watch your hat.
spots/16/kid_tip: A summer-only splash area, 'Moere Beach,' and large play equipment are available.
spots/17/desc: A city park a 10-minute walk from Susukino. Highlights are the October view of maples reflected in Shobuike Pond, the Japanese garden and the Hoheikan Western-style building.
spots/17/access: Directly connected to Nakajima-koen station on the Namboku subway line
spots/17/tip: Good for a morning stroll or a walk to settle your stomach after a meal. In winter, cross-country skis are available to borrow for free.
spots/17/kid_tip: Ducks in the pond, wide lawns, and the nearby children's puppet theater.
spots/18/desc: An observation room on the 38th floor, 173 m above Sapporo Station. Glass on all sides lets you see the whole city and all the way to Ishikari Bay, and you can go up indoors from the station even on rainy days.
spots/18/access: Check in on the 6th floor of JR Tower East, then take the dedicated elevator
spots/18/tip: A good alternative on days you can't go to the Mt. Moiwa night view. The view from the window in the south restroom is famous.
spots/18/kid_tip: ¥520 for junior and senior high students, ¥320 for ages 4 and up, free for ages 3 and under.
spots/19/desc: A shopping complex built on the site of a brewery from 1876. The glass-roofed atrium and the red-brick building are lovely, and it is famous for the giant Christmas tree that goes up from mid-November.
spots/19/access: 3-minute walk from Bus Center-mae station on the Tozai subway line, 15 minutes on foot from Odori
spots/19/tip: With many outdoor brands and household goods, it is useful when you need winter gear in a hurry.
spots/19/kid_tip: A kids' space inside the atrium and wide indoor walkways.
spots/20/desc: A morning market with about 60 stalls next to the central wholesale market. It gets fewer tourists than Nijo Market, crab, sea urchin and melon tend to be cheaper, and the kaisendon at the market restaurants is generous.
spots/20/access: 7-minute walk from Nijuyonken station on the Tozai subway line
spots/20/closed: Varies by shop (many shops close on Wednesdays)
spots/20/tip: After breakfast you can ship seafood home with a delivery service (check item restrictions for shipping to Korea).
spots/20/kid_tip: Kids love the many free samples, but the aisles are narrow, so a baby carrier works better than a stroller.
spots/21/desc: An observation point you reach by lift to the very top of the ski jump built for the 1972 Winter Olympics. The view of the city from the top of the jump is unique, and the museum has a ski jump simulator.
spots/21/access: About 15 minutes by bus from Maruyama-koen subway station; get off at Okurayama Kyogijo Iriguchi
spots/21/hours: Lift generally 9:00–17:00 (varies by season, to be confirmed)
spots/21/closed: Closed on competition and maintenance days (to be confirmed)
spots/21/tip: The ¥1,000 lift round trip and ¥600 museum fee are rough 2024 figures and need to be confirmed. It is in the same western area as Shiroi Koibito Park, so the two pair well.
spots/21/kid_tip: The museum's hands-on corners suit elementary school children and older.
spots/22/desc: A retro terminal still using its 1934 station building. The kerosene-lamp decorations on the platform and the Sankaku Market in front of the station are the sights, and the canal is a gentle 10-minute downhill walk away.
spots/22/access: About 35 minutes from Sapporo Station on the JR Rapid Airport (around ¥750 one way), or about 50 minutes on a local train
spots/22/tip: On the way there, get off at Minami-Otaru Station and walk downhill, then board at this station on the way back so you never have to climb the slope. For sea views, sit on the right side in the direction of travel.
spots/22/kid_tip: Buy the kids a single crab leg at the Sankaku Market in front of the station.
spots/23/desc: The closest station to Marchen Crossing and the Music Box Museum. Get off here and walk down Sakaimachi Street toward the canal for the easiest route.
spots/23/access: About 32 minutes from Sapporo Station on JR (the Rapid Airport stops here)
spots/23/tip: It is about a 10-minute downhill walk from the station to Marchen Crossing. There are few coin lockers, so leave your luggage in Sapporo.
spots/23/kid_tip: The road in front of the station is narrow and has cars, so hold hands.
spots/24/desc: A canal from 1923 lined with stone warehouses and 63 gas lamps. The Asakusabashi Bridge is the classic photo spot, and the moment the gas lamps come on at dusk is the prettiest.
spots/24/hours: Always open. Canal cruise about 40 minutes, ¥1,800 by day and ¥2,000 at night (2024 prices, to be confirmed)
spots/24/closed: None (cruises are cancelled in bad weather)
spots/24/tip: During the Otaru Snow Light Path Festival in February, candles float along the whole canal and it is especially beautiful. The cruise has shorter lines after lunch.
spots/24/kid_tip: Cruise fares for children are separate. The railings along the promenade are low, so hold your child's hand.
spots/25/desc: An old shopping street running about 900 m from the canal to Marchen Crossing. Glass studios and dessert shops such as Kitaichi Glass, LeTAO, Rokkatei and Kitakaro line the street, and just walking it can take half a day.
spots/25/access: 10-minute walk from JR Minami-Otaru Station, 15 minutes from Otaru Station
spots/25/tip: Glass crafts are fragile, so buy them last and ask for cushioned packing. The steam clock at Marchen Crossing sounds every 15 minutes.
spots/25/kid_tip: The LeTAO main shop's 2nd-floor cafe and soft-serve shops all along the street make good rest stops.
spots/26/name: Otaru Music Box Museum, Main Building
spots/26/desc: One of Japan's largest music box specialty shops, in a brick warehouse from 1912. More than 25,000 music boxes fill the three floors, and the steam clock at the entrance is its symbol.
spots/26/access: 10-minute walk from JR Minami-Otaru Station, in front of Marchen Crossing
spots/26/tip: Make-your-own music box workshops are by reservation at the Yuki Experience Studio in the annex. Small music boxes start from around ¥1,500.
spots/26/kid_tip: There is a hands-on exhibit corner on the 2nd floor that children can touch.
spots/27/desc: A 532 m-high observatory overlooking Otaru Port, the city and the Shakotan Peninsula. Counted among Hokkaido's three great night views, the summit has the Tengu Museum and a squirrel park.
spots/27/access: About 17 minutes by Chuo Bus bound for Tenguyama Ropeway from in front of JR Otaru Station
spots/27/hours: Generally 9:30–21:00 (varies by season, to be confirmed)
spots/27/closed: Maintenance closures in spring and autumn (to be confirmed)
spots/27/tip: The ¥1,600 round trip is a rough 2024 figure and needs to be confirmed. Recommended as an evening night-view outing if you stay overnight in Otaru.
spots/27/kid_tip: The summer squirrel park and a winter sledding hill at the summit.
spots/28/desc: A clear caldera lake 40 minutes by car from New Chitose Airport. As Japan's northernmost lake that never freezes, even in winter, it has a lakeside path, boat cruises and day-trip hot springs, and is a good stop on the first or last day of a rental car trip.
spots/28/access: About 40 minutes by rental car from New Chitose Airport, or about 45 minutes by Chuo Bus from Chitose Station (fare to be confirmed)
spots/28/hours: Always open (cruises Apr–Nov generally 8:40–17:10, to be confirmed)
spots/28/tip: The lakeside parking lot is paid (around ¥500, to be confirmed). The 30-minute underwater cruise is so clear you can see the pebbles on the lake bottom.
spots/28/kid_tip: Skipping stones on the lakeside pebble beach, and kayaking in summer.
restaurants/0/desc: The number one pick for a first Sapporo soup curry, with a rich, fragrant broth and a tender chicken leg. You can choose the rice portion and spice level, so kids can have it mild too.
restaurants/1/signature: Crispy chicken leg soup curry with skewered vegetables
restaurants/1/desc: Known for its deep-fried skewered vegetables, which photograph beautifully. It has more seats and faster turnover than Garaku, making it a good dinner alternative.
restaurants/2/desc: Famous for its savory ebi soup made from shrimp heads. You choose a shrimp or chicken broth and stack on toppings, so it is fun for two people to order differently and compare.
restaurants/3/signature: Fresh lamb Genghis Khan, finishing ochazuke
restaurants/3/desc: The symbol of Sapporo Genghis Khan since 1954. At the counter you grill lamb with onions on a cast-iron plate, then finish by pouring tea over rice with the leftover seasoning.
restaurants/3/tips/2: Smell clings to clothes, so put your coat in a plastic bag
restaurants/4/signature: All-you-can-eat-and-drink Genghis Khan and draft beer course
restaurants/4/desc: In the hall of a red-brick former factory, enjoy factory-fresh draft beer and Genghis Khan in a 100-minute all-you-can-eat-and-drink course. It is next to the Beer Museum, so it makes a natural dinner after an afternoon visit.
restaurants/5/desc: Famous for a broth bursting with shrimp aroma that suits Korean tastes well. It is open until late, so it is good for a late-night meal.
restaurants/5/tips/2: Also has a branch at New Chitose Airport's Ramen Dojo
restaurants/6/desc: The classic rich Sapporo miso ramen, topped with a layer of lard that keeps it piping hot to the last bite. The main shop (Nakanoshima) is far away, but the Susukino branch is open late and easy to reach.
restaurants/7/desc: A regular number one in Sapporo miso ramen rankings. The owner trained at Sumire, and you eat the mellow miso broth topped with ginger. It is 20 minutes from downtown by subway.
restaurants/7/hours: 11:00–15:15, 17:00–19:30 (lunch only on some days, to be confirmed)
restaurants/7/closed: Monday, irregular on Tuesday (to be confirmed)
restaurants/8/desc: A conveyor-belt sushi place whose toppings are so good that there is always a line. It is inside the Sapporo Station building, so it is the easiest place to have dinner right after returning from Otaru.
restaurants/8/tips/1: Take a number and go shopping
restaurants/9/desc: An izakaya famous for tsukkomeshi, where staff shout 'Ossha!' and pour salmon roe until the bowl overflows. The show is fun even for two, and the rule is a promise not to leave any rice when you order.
restaurants/10/name: Sapporo Kani Honke, Station-front Main Shop
restaurants/10/signature: Hairy crab and snow crab courses
restaurants/10/desc: A crab specialist serving hairy crab, snow crab and king crab courses in private rooms. It is well known to Korean visitors as a splurge meal and has a Korean-language menu.
restaurants/11/signature: Three-color bowl of sea urchin, salmon roe and crab
restaurants/11/desc: A kaisendon shop where you top your bowl with sea urchin, salmon roe and crab as you like, open from early morning. It is a small shop inside the market, so there is no line if you arrive before 8 a.m.
restaurants/12/desc: A market restaurant with dozens of menu items, so two people can order differently and share. It has roomy seating and a kids' menu, making it a safe family breakfast.
restaurants/13/desc: The main shop of Rokkatei, one of Hokkaido's signature confectioners. Buy souvenirs on the 1st floor, then enjoy main-shop-exclusive desserts and free coffee at the 2nd-floor cafe.
restaurants/13/tips/2: Butter sandwiches need a cooler bag
restaurants/14/desc: A cafe in the former Hokkaido Prefectural Library from 1926, renovated by the architect Tadao Ando. The floor-to-ceiling bookshelves are a photo spot, and the cake set includes coffee, so it is good value.
restaurants/14/hours: Shop 10:00–18:00, cafe 10:00–17:00 (last order 16:30, to be confirmed)
restaurants/15/signature: Premium milk soft serve, freshly baked cheese tart
restaurants/15/desc: The Odori shop of a Sapporo-born pastry maker. The classic move is to take a rich milk soft serve and sit on a bench in Odori Park.
restaurants/15/tips/2: Pairs well with a park stroll
restaurants/16/desc: Sapporo's signature coffee house in a wooden old house covered in ivy. The creaky stairs and lamp lighting are atmospheric, making it ideal for a quiet afternoon after a walk at Hokkaido Shrine.
restaurants/16/tips/1: Few seats, so expect a wait
restaurants/17/desc: The shop that started Sapporo's 'shime parfait' culture of having a parfait as a second stop after dinner. It offers artful parfaits that change with the seasons, with sake and coffee pairings.
restaurants/17/hours: 18:00–24:00 or so (from daytime on weekends, to be confirmed)
restaurants/17/tips/2: Each of you orders a different one
restaurants/18/signature: Lunch set of nigiri with fish from Otaru's coastal waters
restaurants/18/desc: A leading long-established shop on Otaru's Sushi Street, founded in 1938. The lunch set is an easy way to enjoy it, and the private rooms on the 3rd floor are good for family meals.
restaurants/19/desc: A restaurant inside Sankaku Market right next to Otaru Station. Its signature is the 'wagamama-don,' where you pick toppings such as sea urchin, salmon roe and shrimp, and it opens at 8 a.m.
restaurants/20/desc: An Otaru specialty restaurant that fries half a chicken whole. Crispy outside and juicy inside, it goes down well with kids, and the low price makes it a good alternative to sushi.
restaurants/21/desc: The original main shop of the double fromage that started in Otaru. Have a cheesecake set at the 2nd-floor cafe and look down on Marchen Crossing from the rooftop deck.
restaurants/22/signature: Coffee and cake under kerosene lamps
restaurants/22/desc: A warehouse cafe inside Kitaichi Glass Building No. 3, lit only by 167 kerosene lamps. A signature sight is the staff lighting the lamps just after opening in the morning.
restaurants/23/desc: A street on the 3rd floor of New Chitose Airport's domestic terminal with 10 ramen shops from around Hokkaido. You can catch the ramen you missed in the city before your flight.
restaurants/24/signature: Seasonal fruit parfait (chestnut and grape in autumn)
restaurants/24/desc: Together with Sato, one of the two giants of shime parfait, with artful parfaits made from seasonal fruit. A good alternative when the line at Sato is long, and in autumn it serves chestnut and grape parfaits.
restaurants/25/name: Matsuo Jingisukan, New Chitose Airport Branch
restaurants/25/desc: Takikawa-style Genghis Khan, grilling marinated lamb with vegetables. It differs from Daruma's fresh-meat style in the city, so it is nice to compare at the airport on your last day.
hotels/0/desc: A natural hot-spring public bath is perfect for easing tired legs after a day in Otaru, and it is famous for the free late-night soba around 9:30 p.m. and a seafood rice bowl breakfast. It is attached to the Tanukikoji arcade, so both Susukino and Odori are within walking distance.
hotels/0/pts/1: Highly rated by two women traveling together
hotels/1/desc: A hotel with modern, stylish interiors that photograph well. You can end the day with a city view from the top-floor public bath, and being midway between Sapporo Station and Odori, everything is within a 5-minute walk.
hotels/1/pts/1: Close to both the station and Odori
hotels/2/desc: The rooms are on the 23rd floor and above in JR Tower over Sapporo Station, so your window view is the night view. It has a natural hot-spring spa on the 22nd floor, and airport and Otaru JR trips can be done inside the building, which is handy on snowy days.
hotels/2/pts/0: Indoors to the station even in the rain
hotels/2/pts/1: The view is an attraction in itself
hotels/3/desc: A clean, reasonably priced business hotel a 2-minute walk from the south exit of Sapporo Station. The twin rooms are fairly large, so there is room to open two suitcases.
hotels/4/name: Jozankei Tsuruga Resort Spa Mori no Uta
hotels/4/desc: A popular Jozankei hot-spring resort with a forest bonfire lounge, open-air baths and buffet meals included. A free shuttle bus (reservation required) runs from downtown Sapporo, so you can make an overnight hot-spring trip without a rental car.
hotels/4/pts/1: Two meals included, so it feels like good value
hotels/5/desc: Right next to Tanukikoji, with a kitchenette and a large bed in every room, making it an easy hotel to stay at with kids. It has a natural hot-spring public bath and a sauna, and a convenience store is attached on the 1st floor.

bplan/0/desc: An alternative night view on rainy days, or when Mt. Moiwa is closed for maintenance or strong wind. You go straight up indoors from Sapporo Station.
bplan/1/desc: An indoor course that fills a whole rainy afternoon. After the tour, it flows right into Genghis Khan at the neighboring beer garden.
bplan/2/desc: If you have already been to Otaru, or the foliage is at its peak (mid-October), go here on day two instead of Otaru. One hour by bus; day baths from around 12:00.
bplan/3/desc: With kids, it pairs well with Shiroi Koibito Park on the same Tozai line. Many exhibits are indoors, so it works in winter too.
bplan/4/desc: With a rental car, it is 30 minutes from the city. Great for photos with the glass pyramid, artificial mountain and wide lawns, and a splash area in summer.
bplan/5/desc: A 10-minute walk from Susukino. Easy to fit in as a morning stroll before leaving, or a walk after a meal to settle your stomach.
bplan/6/desc: If you have time left in Otaru, this is a night-view observatory reached by a 17-minute bus ride. JR trains back to Sapporo run until around 10 p.m.
bplan/7/desc: Atrium shopping and dining when snow or rain keeps you off the streets. A giant Christmas tree from mid-November.
nearby_alternatives/0/reason: A smaller, more walkable port city in the same Hokkaido. Night views, the morning market and hilly streets are the highlights, so two nights is enough, and it suits a quiet trip
nearby_alternatives/1/reason: If your goal is the Biei hills, Furano lavender and Asahiyama Zoo, use Asahikawa as your base instead of Sapporo. Even better with a rental car
nearby_alternatives/2/reason: A northeastern alternative when direct flights to Hokkaido are expensive or you worry about snow, with similar food (beef tongue, seafood) and hot springs
